title: Dynamic Endocrine Tests: Too Much? Stop It. Too Little? Kick It.
summary: Learn why single hormone values mislead, how suppression and stimulation tests work, how to work up Cushing syndrome and localise it with ACTH, and how acromegaly is confirmed today.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 25 Hit 1 (OGTT suppression for acromegaly; stimulation for GH deficiency), Hit 4 (Cushing screening and ACTH localisation) and Traps 1 and 4. Checked against Giustina 2024, De Marinis 2026, Aversa 2024, Lee 2026 and Hamidi 2026. Hit 1 framing updated: the 2024 consensus confirms acromegaly with IGF-I > 1.3 × ULN plus clinical signs and keeps the OGTT for equivocal cases (register flag rv-acro-ogtt). Not taught: the reviewer’s GHD cut-off (3 µg/L; thresholds are assay-dependent) and “Cushing disease ~68%”.

objectives: Explain why random GH and single cortisol values are unreliable.
Apply the rule: suppress suspected excess, stimulate suspected deficiency.
Outline the Cushing syndrome workup and localise it with ACTH.
State how acromegaly is confirmed under the 2024 consensus.

scenes.title: A GH of 25 — acromegaly?
scenes.altText: A lab slip shows a random growth hormone (GH) of 25 ng/mL; a second slip shows a morning cortisol at the top of the reference range. Two question tokens: “Acromegaly?” and “Cushing syndrome?”. The mascot shrugs: one random value can’t answer either.

cues.text: A random growth hormone comes back at twenty-five. Is this acromegaly?
Another patient has a high-normal morning cortisol. Is this Cushing syndrome?
Neither number answers the question. Hormones that pulse and cycle need a different kind of test.

scenes.title: Normal: pulses, rhythms and feedback
scenes.altText: Left: GH shown as a row of bars of very different heights — secretion comes in bursts, so a random sample can catch a peak or a trough. IGF-I, made mainly in the liver in response to GH, is drawn as a steady line that integrates GH action. Right: a feedback loop — hypothalamus (CRH) → pituitary (ACTH) → adrenal (cortisol), with cortisol feeding back to switch ACTH off. A clock token: cortisol falls to its lowest around midnight.

cues.text: Growth hormone is released in bursts. A random sample can land on a peak or in a trough, so a single value tells you very little.
IGF-I is the steadier signal. GH acts mainly on the liver to make IGF-I, which reflects GH activity over time.
Cortisol runs on a feedback loop. The hypothalamus releases CRH, the pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal makes cortisol — which then switches ACTH off.
Cortisol also follows a daily rhythm, with its lowest point around midnight.

scenes.title: What changes: suppress the excess, stimulate the deficit
scenes.altText: A rule banner: “Suspect excess → try to suppress it. Suspect deficiency → try to stimulate it.” Panel 1: oral glucose normally suppresses GH (bar falls); in acromegaly an autonomous adenoma keeps GH up (nadir ≥ 1 µg/L). Panel 2: GH deficiency — a stimulus (insulin hypoglycemia, glucagon or macimorelin) normally makes GH rise; in deficiency it stays flat. Panel 3: 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 pm normally suppresses morning cortisol; in Cushing syndrome cortisol stays above 1.8 µg/dL (50 nmol/L).

cues.text: The rule for dynamic tests: if you suspect too much hormone, try to suppress it. If you suspect too little, try to stimulate it.
Glucose normally suppresses growth hormone. In acromegaly, the adenoma ignores it, and GH fails to fall below about one microgram per litre.
For suspected GH deficiency, it’s the opposite: give a stimulus — insulin hypoglycemia, glucagon, or macimorelin — and look for GH that fails to rise.
For Cushing syndrome, give one milligram of dexamethasone at night. Normally, next-morning cortisol is suppressed. Above one point eight micrograms per decilitre is a failure to suppress.

scenes.title: In the lab: the Cushing and acromegaly pathways
scenes.altText: Cushing pathway as steps: rule out exogenous glucocorticoids → screen with 1-mg DST, late-night salivary cortisol or 24-h urine free cortisol → confirm with a second test → measure ACTH: < 10 pg/mL = ACTH-independent (adrenal); > 20 pg/mL = ACTH-dependent (pituitary or ectopic); between = grey zone. Caveat token: DST false positives with oral estrogen, CYP3A4 inducers, obesity, alcohol, psychiatric illness. Acromegaly pathway (2024 consensus): IGF-I > 1.3 × upper limit of normal plus typical clinical signs confirms it; OGTT is for equivocal results.

cues.text: Cushing workup. First rule out steroid medicines. Then screen with a 1-milligram dexamethasone test, late-night salivary cortisol, or 24-hour urine free cortisol — and confirm with a second test.
Watch for false positives on the dexamethasone test: oral estrogen, drugs that speed dexamethasone breakdown, obesity, alcohol, and psychiatric illness.
Once cortisol excess is proven, ACTH tells you where to look. Below ten picograms per millilitre: ACTH-independent — the adrenal. Above twenty: ACTH-dependent — pituitary or ectopic.
For acromegaly, current consensus confirms the diagnosis with an IGF-I above 1.3 times the upper limit, plus typical clinical signs. The glucose suppression test is kept for equivocal results.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “A random GH of 25 means acromegaly” is crossed out → “GH pulses; use IGF-I (and OGTT if equivocal).” Trap card: “Low ACTH in Cushing syndrome → image the pituitary” is crossed out → “Low ACTH = ACTH-independent: look at the adrenal.” Trap card: “One abnormal screening test proves Cushing syndrome” is crossed out → “Confirm with a second test and exclude steroids and false positives.”

cues.text: Trap one: a random GH of twenty-five isn’t acromegaly. GH pulses; use IGF-I, and the glucose suppression test if results are equivocal.
Trap two: in proven Cushing syndrome, a low ACTH doesn’t send you to the pituitary. Low ACTH means the adrenal is working on its own.
Trap three: one abnormal screen isn’t a diagnosis. Confirm with a second test, and rule out steroid medicines and false positives first.

scenes.title: Too much? Try to stop it. Too little? Try to kick it.
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Too much? Try to stop it. Too little? Try to kick it.” — like testing a thermostat: if a room is too hot, see whether turning the dial down cools it; if too cold, whether turning it up warms it. A card lists where the analogy breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: too much? Try to stop it. Too little? Try to kick it. Like checking a thermostat — turn it down and see if the room cools, or up and see if it warms.

Where it breaks: cut-offs depend on the assay; drugs, obesity, alcohol and illness cause false results; cyclic Cushing syndrome can test normal between cycles; and some diagnoses — like acromegaly with a clearly high IGF-I — don’t need a dynamic test at all.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Excess → suppress (OGTT, 1-mg DST > 1.8 µg/dL) · deficiency → stimulate”, “Cushing: confirm, then ACTH < 10 adrenal / > 20 pituitary or ectopic · acromegaly: IGF-I”.

cues.text: Test hormone excess by trying to suppress it and deficiency by trying to stimulate it — then use ACTH to localise Cushing syndrome and IGF-I to confirm acromegaly.

props.label: Excess → suppress (OGTT; 1-mg DST > 1.8 µg/dL fails) · deficiency → stimulate
Cushing: ACTH < 10 adrenal · > 20 pituitary/ectopic · acromegaly: IGF-I > 1.3 × ULN

explanation.what: Plain language: hormones that pulse or cycle can’t be judged from one sample, so labs push the system and watch how it responds. Scientific terms: suppression tests (75-g OGTT for GH; 1-mg overnight dexamethasone for cortisol) for suspected excess; stimulation tests (insulin tolerance, glucagon, macimorelin) for suspected GH deficiency. Cushing screening: 1-mg DST (cortisol > 1.8 µg/dL / 50 nmol/L = failure to suppress), late-night salivary cortisol, 24-h urine free cortisol; ACTH < 10 pg/mL = ACTH-independent, > 20 pg/mL = ACTH-dependent.
explanation.why: GH secretion is pulsatile, while IGF-I (made mainly in the liver under GH stimulation) integrates GH action. Normal feedback lets glucose suppress GH and dexamethasone suppress ACTH and cortisol; autonomous tumours ignore the signal. A deficient gland cannot respond to stimulation.
explanation.measure: Acromegaly: IGF-I > 1.3 × ULN plus characteristic signs confirms; OGTT (GH nadir < 1 µg/L, or < 0.4 µg/L with ultrasensitive assays, is the normal response) for equivocal results. Cushing: exclude exogenous glucocorticoids, screen, confirm with a second test, then ACTH. DST false positives: oral estrogen, CYP3A4 inducers, poor absorption, pregnancy, renal impairment, obesity, alcohol, psychiatric illness.
explanation.differs: ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma, low ACTH) vs ACTH-dependent (pituitary Cushing disease or ectopic ACTH, high ACTH). Suppression tests (excess) vs stimulation tests (deficiency).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: random GH traps, OGTT/IGF-I in acromegaly, 1-mg DST cut-off, ACTH localisation, and DST false positives.

analogyLimitations: Bars are schematic and not measured values.
The thermostat analogy ignores pulsatility, circadian rhythm and assay limits.
Thyroid, adrenal-insufficiency and aldosterone testing are not covered here.
takeaway: Test hormone excess by trying to suppress it and deficiency by trying to stimulate it — then use ACTH to localise Cushing syndrome and IGF-I to confirm acromegaly.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected Cushing syndrome takes 1 mg dexamethasone at 11 pm; 8 am serum cortisol is 6.2 µg/dL. Late-night salivary cortisol is also elevated. Plasma ACTH is 4 pg/mL. What is the most likely source?

options.rationale: Correct. Two abnormal screens confirm hypercortisolism, and ACTH < 10 pg/mL points to autonomous adrenal secretion.
Incorrect. Cushing disease gives normal-to-high ACTH.
Incorrect. Ectopic ACTH gives high ACTH.
Incorrect. Cortisol above 1.8 µg/dL after 1 mg dexamethasone is a failure to suppress.

questions.stem: A random GH is 22 ng/mL in a patient without acromegalic features; IGF-I is normal for age and sex. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Likely a physiological GH pulse; a random GH is not diagnostic
options.rationale: Correct. GH is pulsatile; a normal IGF-I argues against acromegaly.
Incorrect. Random GH is not used to diagnose acromegaly.
Incorrect. Deficiency is tested by stimulation, and a high value does not suggest it.

options.text: Repeat a random GH until it is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeated random values do not solve pulsatility; IGF-I or a dynamic test does.

questions.stem: A woman taking an oral estrogen-containing contraceptive has a 1-mg overnight DST cortisol of 2.4 µg/dL but a normal late-night salivary cortisol and normal 24-h urine free cortisol. What is the best explanation?

options.text: A possible false-positive DST caused by the oral estrogen
options.rationale: Correct. Oral estrogen-containing contraceptives are a recognised cause of false-positive DST, and the other two screens are normal.
Incorrect. One abnormal screen with two normal screens does not confirm it.
Incorrect. Failure to suppress does not indicate low cortisol production.
Incorrect. 2.4 µg/dL is above the 1.8 µg/dL cut-off.

references.citation: Giustina A, Biermasz N, Casanueva FF, et al. Consensus on criteria for acromegaly diagnosis and remission. Pituitary. 2024;27(1):7-22.
references.usedFor: IGF-I > 1.3 × ULN for age plus characteristic clinical signs confirms acromegaly; random GH not required; OGTT may be useful for equivocal results; earlier criteria used GH > 1 µg/L during OGTT; IGF-I reflects GH action, primarily in the liver.

references.citation: De Marinis L, Chiloiro S, Mancini A, et al. To test or not to test: what we have learnt from 50 years of dynamic testing in acromegaly. Pituitary. 2026;29(2):67.
references.usedFor: Random GH not useful diagnostically because of pulsatile secretion; GH nadir < 1 ng/mL (or < 0.4 ng/mL with ultrasensitive assays) during OGTT.

references.citation: Aversa LS, Cuboni D, Grottoli S, Ghigo E, Gasco V. A 2024 update on growth hormone deficiency syndrome in adults: from guidelines to real life. J Clin Med. 2024;13(20):6079.
references.usedFor: Adult GHD diagnosed with GH stimulation tests (ITT historically the gold standard; glucagon, macimorelin alternatives); thresholds are assay-dependent.

references.citation: Lee J, Fukuoka H, Park SS, et al. Consensus on the diagnosis of Cushing’s disease: a collaborative statement from the Korean Endocrine Society and Japan Endocrine Society. Endocr J. 2026;73(2):355-366.
references.usedFor: 1-mg ODST at 11 pm, cortisol 8–9 am > 1.8 µg/dL (50 nmol/L) = failure of suppression (~95% sensitivity); ODST false positives with obesity, alcoholism, psychiatric disorders; morning ACTH < 10 pg/mL suggests ACTH-independent and > 20 pg/mL ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome.

references.citation: Hamidi O, St-Jean M, Lacroix A, Bancos I. Measuring cortisol in Cushing syndrome: diagnosis, monitoring, and cortisol circadian rhythm improvement. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2026;111(6):1513-1527.
references.usedFor: Screening with 24-h UFC, LNSC or 1-mg DST; if abnormal, repeat one or two screening tests and exclude non-neoplastic hypercortisolism; DST false positives from oral contraceptives, CYP3A4 inducers, poor absorption, pregnancy, renal impairment; cortisol circadian nadir.

claims.text: GH is pulsatile, so random GH is not diagnostic; IGF-I reflects GH action (liver).
Acromegaly: IGF-I > 1.3 × ULN plus clinical signs confirms; OGTT for equivocal results; normal GH nadir < 1 µg/L (< 0.4 ultrasensitive).
GH deficiency is diagnosed by stimulation tests (ITT, glucagon, macimorelin); thresholds assay-dependent.
1-mg DST: cortisol > 1.8 µg/dL = failure to suppress; confirm with a second screening test; false positives listed.
Oral estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin, raising total cortisol (mechanism of DST false positives).
claims.note: Hamidi 2026 lists oral contraceptives as a cause of false-positive DST; the CBG mechanism was not stated in a consulted source.

claims.text: “Too much? Stop it. Too little? Kick it.”
